story: In 1910 José Urfé added a montuno, the improvised closing section of the son, to his danzón "El bombín de Barreto". The charanga Arcaño y sus Maravillas, led by the flautist Antonio Arcaño, made popular a danzón with a new rhythm. In the mid-to-late 1930s its players said "vamos a mambear", "let's mambo", of the danzón's final improvisation. Arcaño's cellist Orestes López wrote the first danzón called "Mambo", in 1938. Dámaso Pérez Prado went to Mexico in 1949 looking for work and gave the name mambo to a new style. His band had four to five trumpets and four to five saxophones over bass, drums, congas and bongos. Each phrase ended with a deep sound from the throat. In New York the Palladium Ballroom called itself the "temple of mambo". In Cuba the violinist Enrique Jorrín of Orquesta América is credited with creating the cha-cha-chá. Seeing that dancers had trouble with heavy syncopation, he simplified it. He had the band sing in unison so the words carried. In 1951 he wrote the cha-cha-chá "La engañadora". By the 1970s mambo had been largely absorbed into salsa.

sentences.text: In 1910 José Urfé added a montuno, the improvised closing section of the son, to his danzón "El bombín de Barreto".
sentences.quote: in 1910, [[José Urfé]] had first added a [[montuno]] (typical [[Son (music)|son]] improvised closing section) as a final part of his composition ''El bombín de Barreto''

sentences.text: The charanga Arcaño y sus Maravillas, led by the flautist Antonio Arcaño, made popular a danzón with a new rhythm.
sentences.quote: made popular by the [[Charanga (Cuba)|charanga]] Arcaño y sus Maravillas conducted by flautist [[Antonio Arcaño]]

sentences.text: In the mid-to-late 1930s its players said "vamos a mambear", "let's mambo", of the danzón's final improvisation.
sentences.quote: During the mid-to-late 1930s, some members of the Arcaño group were saying ''vamos a mambear'' ("let's mambo") when referring to the montuno or final improvisation of the danzón.

sentences.text: Arcaño's cellist Orestes López wrote the first danzón called "Mambo", in 1938.
sentences.quote: It was Arcaño's cellist, [[Orestes López]], who created the first danzón called "[[Mambo (1938 song)|Mambo]]" (1938).

sentences.text: Dámaso Pérez Prado went to Mexico in 1949 looking for work and gave the name mambo to a new style.
sentences.quote: In 1949 he traveled to Mexico looking for job opportunities and achieved great success with a new style, to which he assigned a name that had been already used by [[Antonio Arcaño]], the ''mambo''.

sentences.text: His band had four to five trumpets and four to five saxophones over bass, drums, congas and bongos.
sentences.quote: an expanded instrumentation consisting of four to five trumpets, four to five saxophones, double bass, drums, maracas, cowbell, congas and bongos

sentences.text: Each phrase ended with a deep sound from the throat.
sentences.quote: stimulated at the end of each musical phrase by a characteristic deep throat sound expression

sentences.text: In New York the Palladium Ballroom called itself the "temple of mambo".
sentences.quote: The Ballroom soon proclaimed itself the "temple of mambo"

sentences.text: In Cuba the violinist Enrique Jorrín of Orquesta América is credited with creating the cha-cha-chá.
sentences.quote: The creation of cha-cha-chá has been traditionally attributed to Cuban composer and violinist [[Enrique Jorrín]], who began his career playing for the [[Charanga (Cuba)|charanga]] band [[Orquesta América]].

sentences.text: Seeing that dancers had trouble with heavy syncopation, he simplified it.
sentences.quote: Jorrín noticed that most of the dancers had some trouble with highly syncopated rhythms and therefore he simplified the musical texture of his pieces

sentences.text: He had the band sing in unison so the words carried.
sentences.quote: Jorrín also asked the members of the orchestra to sing in unison so the lyrics might be heard more clearly

sentences.text: In 1951 he wrote the cha-cha-chá "La engañadora".
sentences.quote: in 1951 he composed a signature cha-cha-chá, "[[La engañadora]]"

sentences.text: By the 1970s mambo had been largely absorbed into salsa.
sentences.quote: by the 1970s it had been largely incorporated into [[salsa music|salsa]]

disagreements: Tree: the record's parents are son, swing and habanera. The article's infobox gives "{{hlist|[[Danzón]]|[[swing music|swing]]|[[son cubano]]}}" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mambo_(music)?action=raw): danzón is the direct parent and is not on the tree; habanera is not mentioned.

Ended: the record says 1960; the article says mambo "continued to enjoy some degree of popularity into the 1960s" and the Palladium closed in 1966 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mambo_(music)?action=raw); cha-cha-chá dates from the early 1950s ("Early 1950s, [[Cuba]]", https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cha-cha-chá_(music)?action=raw).

Origin: Havana matches the infobox ("Late 1930s, [[Havana]]", https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mambo_(music)?action=raw), but the big-band brass mambo of the record's sound was made in Mexico City from 1949 by Pérez Prado (sentence 5), not in Havana.
notes: Sentence 5: Pérez Prado's name is in the article's previous sentence; the quote starts 'In 1949 he traveled'. Sentence 8: the Palladium's name and New York are in the preceding sentences of the same paragraph. Cha-cha-chá sentences (9-12) come from 'Cha-cha-chá (music)'; the URL contains an accented letter, which the check script fetched fine.
